title: Japan Eyes Tighter Crypto Rules for DeFi and Self-Custody Wallets Over Illicit Finance
summary:
Key Takeaways: Japan’s FSA is performing a study on limitations on the use of DeFi. Other responsibilities may be placed on stablecoins at the issuer level. Self-custodial wallets are the
The post Japan Eyes Tighter Crypto Rules for DeFi and Self-Custody Wallets Over Illicit Finance appeared first o...
content:
Key Takeaways:

  • Japan’s FSA is performing a study on limitations on the use of DeFi.
  • Other responsibilities may be placed on stablecoins at the issuer level.
  • Self-custodial wallets are the target of security and fraud scrutiny.

Japan’s Financial Services Agency (FSA) is considering additional regulations for decentralized finance (DeFi) and self-custodial wallets. A discussion paper dated November 26 examines how authorities could strengthen investor protection and combat illicit financial activity without unnecessarily restricting blockchain innovation.

  • Japan Examines Restrictions on DeFi Platforms
  • Stablecoin Issuers Could Face Greater Compliance Responsibilities
    • Japan Reviews Additional Safeguards for Self-Custodial Wallets
    • Growing DeFi Adoption Drives Japan’s Regulatory Review

Japan Examines Restrictions on DeFi Platforms

The FSA will be taking action to incentivize users to not use Defi protocols without proper anti-money laundering (AML) and anti-counter terrorist financing (CFT) protocols.

Among the biggest questions the regulator has is who’s liable to legalised sanctions when seemingly decentralized platforms have elements of centralised control.

Authorities may look at things like governance token concentration, administrative privileges, control over protocol revenue and smart contract upgrades.

The user interface that links investors to decentralized exchanges (DEXs) is also discussed if it ought to be subject to financial regulations such as identity verification and risk disclosure requirements.

The FSA does, however, understand the importance of offering financial services as opposed to creating software that can be utilized for genuine objectives. There have been no blanket regulations on deFi platforms enacted.

Stablecoin Issuers Could Face Greater Compliance Responsibilities

If no responsible party can be located within a DeFi protocol, the regulator is looking at tackling the financial crime concerns via regulated companies that connect with DeFi.

That includes any stablecoin issuers, any services to convert fiat to crypto, or financial institutions.

The method would enhance supervision of major avenues for interaction, rather than directly containing obligations on independent smart contracts, from unregulated protocols to controlled financial services.

Read More: MetaMask Card Expands to Japan, Thailand and Vietnam, Bringing Crypto to Mastercard

Japan Reviews Additional Safeguards for Self-Custodial Wallets

The FSA is also looking at threats surrounding wallets that enable their owners to control their own private keys. Self-custody provides users with the full authority to control their assets, but insufficient security measures and the loss of signing keys can lead to total losses.

Japanese crypto service providers are already implementing processes for self-custodial wallet transactions to collect information and to keep records of the transactions.

Other measures being considered are cooling-off periods for transfers from newly opened exchange accounts, and transaction monitoring and alerts for possible fraudulent payments.

The regulator admitted that, in general, there are few self-custodial wallet users and makers currently regulated in other countries.

Growing DeFi Adoption Drives Japan’s Regulatory Review

The total value locked (TVL) on DeFi protocols has climbed to around $86.64 billion on June 10, 2023, 85% higher than one year ago at $46.86 billion in May 2022, as revealed by the FSA’s cryptocurrency insights.

The agency also referenced a 2026 survey conducted by Coinbase and EY-Parthenon involving 351 institutional investors. Some 56% utilized DeFi protocols or planned to do so by 2028, with just lending and derivatives leading the way as active applications.

Meanwhile, the discussions regarding Japan’s regulations are part of Japan’s onchain finance plan, which included asset tokenization and stablecoin regulation in July 2026.

title: US Wins Forfeiture of $674K in Crypto Tied to an Investment Scam
summary: A federal judge awarded the U.S. government about $674,000 in Tether seized in an online investment scam investigation. Prosecutors said victims can now
content:
A federal judge awarded the U.S. government about $674,000 in Tether seized in an online investment scam investigation. Prosecutors said victims can now seek recovery of stolen funds through the Justice Department’s forfeiture process.

Key Takeaways

  • A federal judge forfeited over 674,739 USDT to the United States.
  • The FBI traced funds from a New York victim to the seized wallet.
  • Prosecutors said victims can seek recovery of their stolen funds.

Federal Judge Orders $674K in Tether Forfeited

The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of New York announced on Nov. 25 that Chief U.S. District Judge Brenda K. Sannes had ordered the forfeiture of seized cryptocurrency to the United States on Nov. 16. The forfeited assets totaled 674,739.480211 USDT, valued at approximately $674,469.58.

First Assistant U.S. Attorney John A. Sarcone III said:

“There is no doubt that the Court’s order comes as a great relief to the victims of this fraud scheme.”

Sannes granted the government’s renewed motion for default judgment and directed the clerk to close the case. The federal court’s forfeiture order followed an initial motion that Sannes denied in March after raising questions about notice to potential claimants and the evidence linking the funds to fraud.

The judge found sufficient evidence to support forfeiture of 275,810.69 USDT as traceable proceeds of wire fraud. The ruling covered the remaining balance under a money laundering provision after the court found that the government had sufficiently linked those funds to transfers intended to conceal the origin of the proceeds.

Failed Withdrawal Led a New York Victim to Discover the Scam

According to the complaint, someone contacted an Onondaga County resident in May 2024 about a platform that purported to teach cryptocurrency trading techniques. The resident transferred funds to what he believed was a secure exchange account linked to the platform and later found he could not withdraw them.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) identified several more victims of the scheme, which prosecutors described as pig butchering. Investigators tracked bitcoin from the New York victim through multiple wallets, where it was mixed with other funds and converted to Tether. The FBI seized the cryptocurrency with help from federal prosecutors.

Separately, the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filed charges over fake trading platforms on Nov. 19 against eight Colorado-based entities. It alleged that people posing as investment advisers provided stock tips before steering investors to fake trading sites, a scheme the agency said caused more than $37 million in losses.

A website can look like a legitimate trading venue while directing deposits to someone else. Common signs of fake crypto exchange scams include sites without an HTTPS connection and offers of guaranteed rewards for opening an account.

Victims Can Seek Recovery of Stolen Funds

The U.S. Attorney’s Office said it generally seeks forfeiture first, then works with the Justice Department’s Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section to return assets to victims in many cases. The Nov. 25 announcement left open the timing and amount of any payments.

In Massachusetts, prosecutors announced a $456,000 crypto forfeiture bid on Nov. 9 after tracing funds allegedly linked to dating site and Facebook fraud to two wallets. That announcement concerned a civil complaint seeking forfeiture of seized USDT.

The Justice Department included cryptocurrency investment fraud among the targets of a nationwide scam enforcement surge spanning 85 federal districts. Prosecutors brought more than 400 criminal cases against more than 800 defendants across the wider effort, which also targeted government impersonation scams.

Craig L. Tremaroli, special agent in charge of the FBI’s Albany Field Office, urged victims to report scams promptly. The FBI’s guidance for crypto scam victims asks victims to give the Internet Crime Complaint Center any wallet addresses, transaction IDs, transfer times, and amounts they have.

title: Japan’s crypto security group taps SEAL to speed up hack response
summary: The partnership comes weeks after a third-party data breach exposed hundreds of thousands of customer email addresses belonging to two Japanese crypto exchanges.
content:
Latest NewsPublishedNov 27, 2026

The partnership comes weeks after a third-party data breach exposed hundreds of thousands of customer email addresses belonging to two Japanese crypto exchanges.

Japan’s crypto industry cybersecurity group has signed an agreement with US nonprofit Security Alliance (SEAL) to improve the detection of cyberattacks and respond to incidents more effectively.

According to a statement released Friday, the memorandum will see JPCrypto-ISAC receive help from SEAL to develop an incident response support framework and give them access to SEAL’s incident response and support capabilities. Both organizations will also share cyber threat intelligence.

In the Web3 and digital asset sector, addressing cyber threats that transcend national borders has become essential, said JPCrypto-ISAC representative director Naoji Noda. “We are delighted to establish this partnership with SEAL through this MOU.”

JPCrypto-ISAC had 16 full members at launch in 2025, including SBI VC Trade, bitbank, GMO Coin and Rakuten Wallet. The organization helps Japanese crypto companies share and analyze cyber threat intelligence.

Earlier this month, Japanese crypto exchanges Zaif and CoinTrade disclosed that a breach at their email provider, Arara, exposed hundreds of thousands of customer email addresses.

Arara estimated that the breach may have affected up to 380 companies across its customer base.

Japan’s crypto industry suffered a major breach in May 2024, when hackers stole Bitcoin worth about $305 million at the time from crypto exchange DMM Bitcoin. US and Japanese authorities later attributed the theft to North Korean hackers.

title: Binance Hacker Moves $35.5M in Ethereum, With $1.9B in Stolen Crypto Still Unfrozen
summary:
Key Takeaways: Hacker wallets belonging to Binance transfer $35.52 million worth of ETH. Almost 19 million bitcoins and almost 10 million ether, worth nearly $1.9 billion, are yet to be
The post Binance Hacker Moves $35.5M in Ethereum, With $1.9B in Stolen Crypto Still Unfrozen appeared first on Cry...
content:
Key Takeaways:

  • Hacker wallets belonging to Binance transfer $35.52 million worth of ETH.
  • Almost 19 million bitcoins and almost 10 million ether, worth nearly $1.9 billion, are yet to be unfrozen.
  • The United States Department of Justice is requesting $1.1 billion in immunity be forfeited.

Wallets linked to the October Binance hack have resumed moving stolen cryptocurrency, with Onchain Lens identifying fresh Ethereum transfers worth $35.52 million on November 26. The activity comes amid ongoing efforts by investigators and stablecoin issuers to recover billions of dollars in stolen digital assets.

BINANCE HACKER IS ON THE MOVE AGAIN

So far, the hacker has moved 35.52M worth $ETH in the past few hours.

Current Unlocked holding:

→ 461.98K $ETH (~$785.2M)
→ 18.35K $BTC (~$1.11B)

Frozen holding: $2.6B in stablecoins

Is Lazarus planning to launder funds again using tornado?

powered by @rainbetcom

— Onchain Lens (@OnchainLens) November 26, 2026

  • Bitcoin Accounts for Nearly 59% of Unfrozen Binance Hack Funds
  • US Authorities Pursue $1.1 Billion in Stolen USDC
    • Frozen Crypto Does Not Mean Recovered Funds
    • Binance Restores Withdrawals While Investigators Track Stolen Assets

Bitcoin Accounts for Nearly 59% of Unfrozen Binance Hack Funds

Onchain Lens reveals that the attacker still holds around 461,980 ETH worth of $785.2 million and 18,350 BTC worth of $1.11 billion.

Bitcoin represents nearly 59% of the combined unfrozen holdings, while Ethereum accounts for the remaining 41%. In addition, the blockchain analytics platform also spotted $2.6 billion of frozen stablecoins.

The recent Ethereum transfers are part of a much greater chain of transactions that occurred in early November. Then, the stolen wallets traded around $142.1 million of ETH on November 18 and just an additional $248.23 million on November 19.

Onchain Lens noted that the tokens could be going back into Tornado Cash, but they weren’t sure where or why. Transfers of cryptocurrency from wallet to wallet aren’t always proof the currency has been sold, converted or successfully laundered.

Read More: Binance $5.5B Hack Exposed: 50 EIP-7702 Nonces Opened One Hot Wallet in Minutes

US Authorities Pursue $1.1 Billion in Stolen USDC

The renewed activity is days after the US Department of Justice’s (DOJ) civil forfeiture motion against over $1.1 billion in USDC suspected to have been connected to the Binance hack.

The Nov. 23 filing lists 36 blockchain addresses on 18 blockchains. The stablecoins issued by the Circle were already affected by a court order banning their transferability.

On October 25, U.S. officials blamed the attack on North Korean cybercriminals who hail from a group known as Lazarus Group.

Frozen Crypto Does Not Mean Recovered Funds

Nearly $3 billion in cryptocurrency has been recently frozen, seized or returned thanks to authorities, the DOJ stated.

This number includes what are referred to as assets in various stages of recovery, though. Frozen stablecoins do not automatically come back to Binance, they can be subject to legal action.

Native cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum are mostly impossible to directly taken offline by a token issuer, adding further difficulties in asset recovery.

Read More: Binance Reveals How Hackers Moved $6.34B After Breaching Its Wallet-Signing System

Binance Restores Withdrawals While Investigators Track Stolen Assets

Binance said the estimated financial damages from their October 29 security hack were about $6.34 billion, and that they would use company funds to rectify damages to customers.

As of October 31, the exchange said they had replenished 98% of the tokens affected and were continuing to buy less liquid cryptocurrencies in early November.

Binance announced on November 27 that they had ended all suspension of withdrawals related to the security incident.

The exchange assures that customers’ assets are 100 percent backed, though some blockchain networks are temporarily unavailable for unrelated maintenance or upgrades.

title: Ethereum devs set Glamsterdam’s Hoodi rollout for mid-December after delays
summary: Glamsterdam’s Hoodi upgrade was delayed in October after concerns that changes to gas pricing could break some existing smart contracts.
content:
Latest NewsPublishedNov 27, 2026

Glamsterdam’s Hoodi upgrade was delayed in October after concerns that changes to gas pricing could break some existing smart contracts.

Ethereum core developers have scheduled the Glamsterdam upgrade for the Hoodi testnet on Dec. 15, nearly two months after it was originally due to go live.

Among a number of upgrades, Glamsterdam changes how much gas Ethereum charges for certain operations under two proposals, EIP-8037 and EIP-8038. However, testing found that under the new rules, some smart contracts could run out of gas and fail, prompting developers to delay the Hoodi rollout originally set for Oct. 26.

In an All Core Developers Consensus call on Thursday, Ethereum developers set Dec. 15 for Glamsterdam’s activation on the Hoodi testnet. Execution-layer teams reached broad agreement to keep EIP-8037 as written after some developers warned that revising the gas pricing proposal could break other smart contracts and further delay the mainnet rollout.

Ethereum researcher and core developer Ansgar Dietrichs said leaving the question open would have pushed the Hoodi rollout into 2027. “Indecision is also just a decision in itself; it would just mean we delay into the next year,” he said.

Ethereum’s Glamsterdam upgrade made it to the Sepolia testnet on Oct. 6, while Hoodi is the final testnet before it goes to mainnet.

The upgrade aims to advance Ethereum’s layer-1 scaling roadmap with enshrined proposer-builder separation, block-level access lists and changes to gas pricing that better reflect the cost of execution.

Last week, Ethereum Foundation’s Rahul Kothari said mid-January would be the earliest viable date for a mainnet rollout, and that the three projects with the highest-severity compatibility issues had either applied fixes or expected to do so by mid-December.

Some projects with medium-severity issues had given timelines as late as Jan. 10.

title: Rickards Warns of AI Trade Collapse as Nvidia’s Comeback Rally Fades
summary: James Rickards predicted that Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO would briefly lift stocks but fail to prevent a collapse in the AI trade. Nvidia gave
content:
James Rickards predicted that Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia CEO would briefly lift stocks but fail to prevent a collapse in the AI trade. Nvidia gave back about 40% of its initial gain over the next two sessions.

Key Takeaways

  • Rickards warned Huang’s return would fail to stop an AI trade collapse.
  • Nvidia gave back about 40% of its Nov. 23 gain by Nov. 25.
  • Booker sought records as plaintiffs moved for a $290 million settlement.

Rickards Warns Nvidia’s Comeback Rally Will Fade

Financial commentator James Rickards warned on Nov. 23 that Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as chief executive of Nvidia (Nasdaq: NVDA) would provide only a short-lived lift to stocks. He argued that the leadership change would do little to address the financing practices he blamed for the AI trade’s vulnerability.

Rickards wrote on X:

“Reinstating Jensen Huang is a one-day wonder for the stock market but it won’t stop the slide and collapse of the AI circle finance Ponzi.”

Nvidia shares jumped 31.5% to $165.05 after Huang returned as CEO, then closed at $155.38 on Nov. 24 and $149.30 on Nov. 25. Nvidia gave back about 40% of its gain on reinstatement day but remained about 19% above its Nov. 20 close.

Bitcoin briefly climbed to $64,505 on Nov. 23 after Huang’s reinstatement. The decline below $60,000 on Nov. 25 came as the Nasdaq Composite closed lower.

The link between stocks and crypto can strengthen when investors reduce exposure to both markets. Nvidia still held part of its Nov. 23 gain by the Nov. 25 close, while bitcoin was down 7.41% from its Nov. 23 peak by that afternoon.

AI Financing Draws Senate Scrutiny

U.S. Senator Cory Booker (D-NJ), the top Democrat on the Senate Judiciary antitrust subcommittee, asked Nvidia for records on Nov. 25 about Trump administration contacts with the board and any discussions of export controls or antitrust enforcement. He asked Nvidia to preserve relevant records dating to Jan. 1 and respond by Dec. 16.

Booker argued that Nvidia’s investments in customers that buy its chips could steer purchases away from competitors. Rickards’ Nov. 23 post went further by alleging a Ponzi scheme, a claim that remains unproven. The proposed AI infrastructure financing platforms announced in August aim to mobilize more than $500 billion in third-party capital through independent underwriting. The proposals were subject to final agreements.

Nvidia’s board voted unanimously to reinstate Huang after receiving input from senior U.S. officials and said its independent inquiry would continue.

Five Senate Democrats asked the administration to explain its role on Nov. 24, seeking details about the officials involved and any intelligence assessments behind the decision.

Huang is scheduled for a transcribed House interview Dec. 1, followed by Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter’s interview Dec. 2. Huang is due to appear at a public Senate Banking Committee hearing on export controls Dec. 3.

Nvidia Reaches $290 Million Settlement in Crypto Mining Suit

Nvidia and Huang reached a proposed $290 million settlement with investors who sued in December 2018, and the investors asked a federal court on Nov. 24 for preliminary approval. The lawsuit alleges that Nvidia obscured how much graphics chip demand came from cryptocurrency miners. Both sides accepted a mediator’s settlement recommendation on Sept. 24, before Huang resigned Nov. 12. The deal still needs a judge’s approval, and Nvidia and Huang deny any wrongdoing.

Rickards also warned about litigation in a War Room interview clip, saying:

“The trillion-dollar class-action lawsuits against Nvidia aren’t going away. Jensen Huang may be back, but he’d better be ready to spend his life in depositions and courtrooms.”

The shareholder complaint filed Nov. 9 against Nvidia and Huang seeks unspecified damages. On Nov. 23, court records show that judges filed referrals concerning two other cases to determine whether they are related to the Nov. 9 suit.

title: Ethereum’s Co-Founder Takes On Crypto’s Next Security Threat. Who Is Vitalik Buterin?
summary: Key takeaways Vitalik Buterin’s November 26 essay argues that crypto security must extend to the physical chips inside devices, summed up as “Not your silicon, not your keys.” He wants manufacturers to publish physical chip layouts (GDS files) so investigators can compare real hardware against the d...
content:
Key takeaways

  • Vitalik Buterin’s November 26 essay argues that crypto security must extend to the physical chips inside devices, summed up as “Not your silicon, not your keys.”
  • He wants manufacturers to publish physical chip layouts (GDS files) so investigators can compare real hardware against the design.
  • Researcher Andrew Huang’s infrared inspection technique (IRIS) can examine chips without removing them, but it has resolution limits and is not a universal fix.
  • The essay is a proposal, not a claim that existing hardware wallets are compromised, and publishing it does not give Buterin power to change Ethereum unilaterally.
  • Arkham attributes about $390 million in assets to Buterin, mostly roughly 224,000 ETH, though his true net worth is not publicly established.

Who is Vitalik Buterin, and why is Ethereum’s co-founder now questioning the security of the very devices crypto investors use to protect their wealth? The 32-year-old programmer has turned his attention to a problem that even open-source software cannot necessarily solve: compromised computer chips.

In an essay published on November 26, Buterin argued that cryptocurrency security needs to extend beyond software and into the physical hardware on which it runs. His message builds on one of crypto’s oldest principles, but with a new twist:

“

Not your silicon, not your keys.

Vitalik Buterin · Essay, November 26

For someone who helped build an alternative to centralized financial infrastructure, questioning the manufacturers behind that infrastructure seems like a natural next step.

It also reflects a security philosophy that has become increasingly visible in Buterin’s work, from his push for greater privacy and quantum safety on Ethereum’s roadmap to his interest in independently verifiable computing.

Who Is Vitalik Buterin?

Vitalik Buterin is a Russian-Canadian programmer, researcher and writer who conceived Ethereum in 2013, at the age of 19.

Born in Russia in 1994 and raised in Canada, Buterin discovered Bitcoin in 2011. He went on to co-found Bitcoin Magazine, where he explored the technology and economics behind cryptocurrencies long before digital assets attracted mainstream financial institutions.

His involvement in Bitcoin exposed him to a problem that would eventually lead to Ethereum. Blockchain technology had potential beyond transferring money, but building more sophisticated applications on Bitcoin presented technical limitations.

Rather than trying to accommodate every possible application within Bitcoin’s existing architecture, Buterin began working on a blockchain designed specifically for programmability.

At the time, he was studying computer science at the University of Waterloo, where he also worked as a research assistant to cryptographer Ian Goldberg.

According to the University of Waterloo, Buterin received a $100,000 Thiel Fellowship in 2014 and subsequently left university to work on Ethereum full-time.

How Vitalik Buterin Created Ethereum

In November 2013, Buterin wrote the initial draft of what would become the Ethereum whitepaper.

The proposal described a blockchain with a general-purpose programming environment. Developers would no longer need to create an entirely new network every time they wanted to build a decentralized application.

Consider a lending platform. Instead of relying on a bank to manage collateral, calculate interest and authorize withdrawals, developers could encode those rules into smart contracts running on Ethereum.

That does not eliminate every risk. Smart contracts can contain bugs, depend on unreliable external data or operate under centralized administrative controls. What Ethereum introduced was the ability to execute financial and other programmable agreements on a shared blockchain.

Although Buterin originated the concept, Ethereum was not built by him alone. Its founding team included seven other individuals: Gavin Wood, Joseph Lubin, Charles Hoskinson, Anthony Di Iorio, Mihai Alisie, Jeffrey Wilcke and Amir Chetrit.

The project’s first live network, known as Frontier, launched on July 30, 2015.

What began as an experimental computing platform eventually became the foundation for much of the decentralized finance industry. Stablecoins, decentralized exchanges, lending protocols and tokenized financial assets now use the infrastructure that Buterin and Ethereum’s early contributors helped establish.

The network’s own evolution, particularly its transition to proof-of-stake and the development of Layer 2 scaling networks, has shaped Ethereum’s first decade.

Vitalik Buterin’s Latest Warning: Can Crypto Wallets Really Be Trusted?

A hardware wallet is supposed to keep private keys away from potentially compromised computers and smartphones. But what happens if the device itself cannot be trusted?

Buterin’s latest research examines that possibility. He points to supply chain attacks involving tampered wallets and considers the potential for malicious modifications concealed inside apparently legitimate chips.

Open-source firmware allows researchers to examine the instructions a device runs. But those instructions reveal little about whether the manufactured chip has been altered.

Buterin wants manufacturers to disclose physical chip layouts, known as GDS files, so investigators have a reference against which to inspect actual hardware.

The distinction matters. Knowing what a chip is designed to do is not necessarily the same as knowing what the chip inside your wallet actually does.

The Technology That Could Help Detect Compromised Chips

One approach highlighted by Buterin comes from hardware security researcher Andrew Huang, better known as bunnie.

Huang has been developing a technique called Infra-Red, In Situ inspection (IRIS), which exploits the fact that silicon becomes transparent at certain infrared wavelengths.

Using infrared illumination and suitable imaging equipment, researchers can examine parts of a chip’s internal structure without necessarily removing it from its circuit board.

The technique could help detect substituted components or unexpected differences between manufactured chips and their intended designs.

However, it is not a universal solution.

In a 2024 update on his research, Huang explained that infrared imaging has resolution limits. It cannot reliably reveal every microscopic feature of modern chips. Combining imaging with additional electrical testing could improve confidence in a component’s integrity.

That is an important limitation for crypto investors. Publishing an open hardware design does not automatically make a wallet secure, just as publishing a smart contract’s code does not establish that it is free of vulnerabilities.

Buterin acknowledges that sophisticated hardware inspections are more likely to be performed by specialist organizations than ordinary wallet owners.

His essay is a proposal for improving security, not an announcement that existing hardware wallets have all been compromised.

Does Vitalik Buterin Control Ethereum?

Despite his status as Ethereum’s most recognizable co-founder, Buterin is not its CEO.

Ethereum is maintained through the participation of independent developers, researchers, node operators, validators and other ecosystem contributors. Changes to the network involve technical proposals, discussion, software development and adoption by participants.

Buterin has considerable influence over those discussions, but publishing a proposal does not give him the authority to implement it unilaterally.

His role within the Ethereum Foundation is also distinct from control over the blockchain itself. In its April 2025 governance announcement, the Foundation described Buterin’s responsibilities as providing technical and intellectual guidance to the wider ecosystem.

His research can influence the direction Ethereum takes. Whether the network ultimately follows that direction depends on considerably more than his endorsement.

How Much Is Vitalik Buterin Worth?

Buterin accumulated considerable wealth through his involvement in Ethereum, with much of his publicly visible cryptocurrency wealth tied to ETH.

However, his exact net worth is not publicly established.

Blockchain analytics can estimate the value of assets held in wallets attributed to him, but those figures do not necessarily account for all his investments, liabilities, private assets or holdings at addresses that have not been publicly identified.

They also fluctuate with cryptocurrency prices. A wallet valuation should therefore not be confused with a complete assessment of his personal wealth.

What Is Vitalik Buterin’s Vision for the Future of Crypto?

Buterin’s latest essay is part of a longer-running interest in making digital infrastructure independently verifiable.

In September 2025, he published The Importance of Full-Stack Openness and Verifiability, exploring how transparency could extend across the hardware and software underpinning increasingly important parts of people’s lives.

His broader research includes cryptography, privacy, blockchain scalability and Ethereum’s transition toward greater quantum resistance. Buterin has previously called for greater experimentation across Ethereum’s application layer without compromising its core principles of censorship resistance, open-source development, privacy and security.

These interests share a practical concern: whether users can independently establish that the systems they rely on behave as intended.

There is a commercial obstacle, though. Semiconductor manufacturers invest heavily in proprietary processes, and designing chips specifically for inspectability can involve performance compromises.

But a device signing a cryptocurrency transaction does not necessarily need the computing power of a modern AI processor. That makes security-focused hardware a potentially useful starting point.

More than a decade ago, Buterin challenged the idea that blockchains should primarily be used to transfer money. His latest work challenges another assumption the industry has grown comfortable with: that trusting the code is enough.

For crypto investors, the next meaningful development may come from hardware manufacturers willing to make their products independently inspectable, rather than another software update promising greater security.

title: BNB Chain Unveils New Layer-1 Blockchain Targeting 100,000 TPS Without a New Token
summary:
Key Takeaways: The new Layer-1 of BNB Chain will achieve 100,000 transactions per second. The network is centered around trading and payments, along with privacy and AI agents. No new
The post BNB Chain Unveils New Layer-1 Blockchain Targeting 100,000 TPS Without a New Token appeared first on Crypto...
content:
Key Takeaways:

  • The new Layer-1 of BNB Chain will achieve 100,000 transactions per second.
  • The network is centered around trading and payments, along with privacy and AI agents.
  • No new token launch for BNB as it will continue to exist as the native token.

BNB Chain has unveiled a litepaper detailing its next-generation Layer-1 blockchain, designed to handle demanding financial applications with faster transaction processing and greater privacy. The network will coexist with BNB Smart Chain (BSC) instead of replacing the existing blockchain.

  • BNB Chain Targets 100,000 TPS With New Blockchain Architecture
  • BNB Chain Introduces Private Crypto Settlement and AI Agent Controls
    • Users Could Pay Network Fees Without Holding BNB
    • BNB Remains Central to the New Layer-1 Ecosystem

BNB Chain Targets 100,000 TPS With New Blockchain Architecture

The proposed network aims to achieve 100,000 transactions per second (TPS), targeting applications that require rapid execution, including high-frequency crypto trading and real-time payments.

It’s designed to partition the ordering of transactions from the execution of them, enabling the network to examine and organize new blocks without blocking previous ones.

The design includes 200ms block length and carries smaller transaction batches, referred to as SubBlocks, about every 20ms. These give early indicators of what transaction placement occurs, not what it can be guaranteed to accomplish.

Normally, finality would be expected to occur in about half a second with network roundtrip time, before waiting for the transaction to be included.

One of the key features is there are separate lanes for transactions. Payment services and trading platforms may be granted reserved blockspace, decreasing competition with other network activities when network congestion occurs. If there was no usage of that capacity, it would be available for other applications as well.

BNB Chain Introduces Private Crypto Settlement and AI Agent Controls

The technology is simple yet reliable and will let its users stake and vault BNB and supported BEP-20 tokens in a confidential pool. Shielded assets could then be directly used to interact with specific decentralized finance (DeFi) services via a mechanism called AtomicCall.

But the system cannot give a full degree of transaction anonymity. Some payouts and public interactive activity on smart contracts as well as transaction fee costs remain onchain.

Read More: Coinbase Launches AI Agent Sign-Ups for Crypto Trading With Built-In Safety Limits

Users Could Pay Network Fees Without Holding BNB

Native account abstraction adds passkey authentication, batching, delegated permissions and fee sponsorship to the protocol. Paymaster services could accept stablecoin compensation and settle fees in BNB, and applications may include transaction fees for users.

Users have also the ability to give limited transactions’ access to autonomous AI agents and grant access when needed, and revoke access when needed, without losing control of their wallets.

BNB Remains Central to the New Layer-1 Ecosystem

BNB Chain has also announced that it will have BNB as a separate native currency, which will serve as its transaction fee, stake, and governance, unlike any other blockchain.

The network will be EVM compatible, but there may be variations in transaction format, calculating fees, and when they are executed.

According to the litepaper, an official cross chain bridge from BSC to the new Layer-1 will soon be implemented with Devnet-2. It’s in development which will be followed by a public testnet.

title: Coinbase Wallet Returns $250K in Trading Fee Rebates to Users
summary: Coinbase Wallet says it has returned $250,000 in trading fees since launching its loyalty program. Its latest weekly payout was $46,000 in USDC, with
content:
Coinbase Wallet says it has returned $250,000 in trading fees since launching its loyalty program. Its latest weekly payout was $46,000 in USDC, with rebate rates based on each trader’s qualifying volume over 30 days.

Key Takeaways

  • Coinbase Wallet returned $250,000 in trading fees since launch.
  • The latest weekly payout sent $46,000 in USDC to traders.
  • Eligible 30-day volume determines rebate rates of up to 50%.

Coinbase Wallet Sends $46,000 in Weekly USDC Rebates

Coinbase Wallet said on Nov. 25 that it had returned $250,000 to traders since its loyalty program began in mid-October. The wallet service from crypto exchange Coinbase (Nasdaq: COIN) told traders to check their wallets for the week’s payout.

Coinbase Wallet wrote on X:

“$250,000 back to Coinbase Wallet traders since the launch of our loyalty program in mid-October. We just sent another $46,000 in USDC fee rebates. Check your wallet to see what you earned this week.”

The program pays rebates in Circle’s dollar-backed stablecoin, USDC. Coinbase Wallet generally groups rebates into Wednesday payouts. Users may need to link a Coinbase account or complete identity, enrollment, or tax requirements, depending on their jurisdiction and annual rebate amount.

Trading Volume Sets the Rebate Rate

The Coinbase Wallet rebate terms set five tiers based on eligible volume over the previous 30 days. Rebates begin at 15% at $5,000, rise to 30% at $25,000 and 40% at $100,000, and reach 50% at $500,000. Volume below $5,000 earns no rebate.

Eligible swaps and perpetuals trades can count when they generate a fee. The wallet applies the trader’s rate to the fee it keeps after discounts and any share that goes to a third-party protocol. Rebates are capped at $10,000 per trade, with no weekly, monthly, or lifetime cap per user.

Participation depends on location, age, and any required identity checks. The terms list the United Kingdom and Singapore among excluded jurisdictions. The wallet may show a pending rebate before settlement and can adjust or reverse payments for errors or abuse.

How Wallet Rebates Fit Into Coinbase Trading

Within the wallet, eligible swaps between crypto assets can qualify based on the fee Coinbase Wallet collects. Fee-free trades generally do not count toward volume, and network or protocol costs can still apply. Where benefits can be combined, payouts cannot exceed the fees the wallet collected.

In the main Coinbase app, integrated decentralized exchange trading had expanded to 84 countries by March, giving users access to tokens beyond the exchange’s listed assets.

Coinbase Advanced applies its own volume-based trading fee tiers. Under the fee structure described in October, lower commissions start at $10,000, and qualifying spot and derivatives trades both count toward the threshold.

Coinbase-backed Base introduced another change for onchain traders in September. The network’s Cobalt upgrade added conditional transactions, allowing users to sign and submit a swap that becomes eligible for execution when a preset price is reached before a deadline they choose.

title: AI is driving a flood of crypto bug reports. Now it’s helping sort them
summary: Bug bounty platform HackerOne said it’s increasing its triage throughput with AI agents after a record quarter of reports in the third quarter.
content:
Crypto bug bounty platforms have expanded their use of artificial intelligence to keep up with a growing mountain of AI-assisted security reports.

Crypto-focused HackenProof said in October that it was using AI to triage 70% of submissions fully autonomously, aiming to hit 85% by the end of 2026. It said it received an average of about 6,100 bug reports a month in the third quarter, 2.4 times the reports from December last year.

Rival Immunefi last week said submissions to its platform rose 136% year-over-year in the first nine months of 2026, as it introduced a tool that can flag duplicates before a researcher submits a report.

Bug bounty programs pay independent researchers to find and report potential security flaws. AI has helped researchers uncover more genuine vulnerabilities, but has also swelled the volume of invalid and duplicate submissions, making it harder for security teams to identify the threats that need urgent attention.

It’s like “bringing a sword to a gunfight,” Dmitry Tokarev, founder of crypto wallet provider Bron, told Cointelegraph, referring to security teams that haven’t already adopted AI to sift through reports.

The turning point for AI-assisted bug hunting

Several bug bounty platforms have identified February as a turning point in the surge of AI-assisted vulnerability reports, coinciding with the release of more capable AI models, including Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.6.

HackenProof said Claude Opus 4.6 could work through larger codebases and sustain tasks for longer. HackerOne said the arrival of more capable AI models and tools in that month saw a sudden shift from a “human-only submission environment.”

Some crypto developers are also experimenting with financial disincentives to curb low-quality submissions.

The team behind Firedancer, a Solana validator client developed by Jump Crypto, which also uses AI to screen reports, took an additional measure in October.

To deter spam, it began requiring researchers to burn 1 SOL for each bug report they want considered for a bounty. The token is permanently destroyed, even if the report turns out to be a duplicate.

In a November update published Tuesday, HackerOne’s vice president of operations Tony Lee said they began requiring researchers to verify their identities before submitting reports in the third quarter. It also expanded its triage team and began using AI agents to automatically close clear-cut cases, such as spam and duplicate reports.

In October, it gave customers more control over how many reports their public programs receive.

Related: AI labs likely sitting on cryptography ‘bombshells,’ computer scientist says

Security teams brace for more bug reports and attacks

Lee said he expects vulnerability reports to keep climbing “for the foreseeable future” after recording a 22% increase in report volume in Q3 compared to the previous quarter.

Meanwhile, insurer QBE and risk consultancy Control Risks on Wednesday forecast more disruptive cyber incidents in 2027 across the 14 markets they studied, pointing to the “industrialization of AI” as one of the factors.

Mike Blank, chief product officer at blockchain infrastructure firm R3, also said he expects the number of hacks to rise sharply in 2027, but said crypto teams should pay closer attention to how much damage a single breach can cause, rather than the number of attacks.

“The real difference will be between protocols where a stolen key can drain everything and those where it can only pause operations,” Blank said.

title: Bitcoin Could Rally Sharply if AI Stocks Recover, Devere CEO Says
summary: Bitcoin could rebound sharply if investors regain confidence in artificial intelligence stocks, the chief executive of Devere Group said. The outlook
content:
Bitcoin could rebound sharply if investors regain confidence in artificial intelligence stocks, the chief executive of Devere Group said. The outlook followed two days of losses for Nvidia and a partial rebound for Anthropic.

Key Takeaways

  • Devere’s CEO sees room for a sharp bitcoin rally if AI stocks recover.
  • Nvidia fell 9.5% over two sessions, while Anthropic rebounded Wednesday.
  • Chipmaker earnings and the Fed’s next decision could shape bitcoin’s next move.

Nvidia Gives Back Part of Its Rally as Anthropic Bounces

Nigel Green, chief executive officer of financial advisory firm Devere Group, said on Nov. 26 that bitcoin could be among the first assets to rally if confidence in AI stocks returns. He expects the cryptocurrency’s moves to remain closely tied to chip stocks in the coming weeks.

Green said:

“Bitcoin is on the Nasdaq leash again. Right now, it trades like a supercharged version of the AI trade.”

Nvidia (Nasdaq: NVDA) fell 3.9% to $149.30 on Nov. 25, its second straight decline after Jensen Huang returned as CEO. The stock closed 9.5% below its Nov. 23 finish of $165.05. The Nasdaq Composite fell 0.6% Wednesday.

Anthropic (Nasdaq: ANT) rose 1.1% to $82.79 after touching $73.85 intraday. It still closed below its $83 initial public offering price and about 15% below its first-day close of $97.17.

Bitcoin recovered to around $61,000 on Nov. 26, after a sell-off ahead of Thanksgiving took it to $57,209 on Bitstamp the previous day. U.S. stock markets were closed for the holiday, while bitcoin continued trading.

After Huang’s reinstatement on Nov. 23, bitcoin’s jump to $64,505 faded within hours. Devere cited a correlation of 0.67 between daily moves in bitcoin and the Nasdaq Composite over the 30 trading days through Nov. 16.

Why Funds May Sell Bitcoin Alongside Tech Stocks

The Devere CEO described how funds manage their holdings:

“It comes down to who owns bitcoin today. It sits in the same portfolios and on the same risk systems as the big AI names. When a fund needs to cut exposure fast, it sells whatever is most liquid and has run the hardest, and bitcoin ticks both boxes.”

Bloomberg Intelligence counted 2,223 filers with spot bitcoin ETF holdings worth $29.8 billion as of Sept. 30. Investment advisers represented about 84% of those filers and accounted for $13.4 billion of the total.

Farside Investors’ daily bitcoin ETF flow data showed $453 million in net outflows from U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs on Nov. 25, the seventh straight trading day of withdrawals. November net outflows reached about $5.39 billion through Nov. 25. The flow figures do not identify which investors sold or why.

Bitcoin can trade around the clock, and liquidity across bitcoin exchanges varies by venue and trading pair. That affects how much a fund can sell near the prevailing price when it needs to raise cash quickly.

What Could Support a Broader AI Stock Recovery

Green expects chipmaker earnings, demand for AI computing, and the next Federal Reserve decision to have more influence on bitcoin over the next few weeks than developments on its network. He believes the link between bitcoin and tech shares will weaken once concerns about AI valuations ease.

Chipmakers’ sales forecasts could show whether demand for AI computing is growing fast enough to support stock valuations. The Federal Reserve’s December meeting on Dec. 8 and 9 follows a rise in annual inflation to 3.8% in October on the Fed’s preferred measure.

Trade policy added another source of uncertainty. The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative outlined proposed Section 301 actions on Nov. 25 covering 14 economies, including China and the European Union, after finding their manufacturing policies burdened or restricted U.S. commerce.

“Leashes don’t last forever. Bitcoin’s ties to tech stocks have tightened and loosened many times, and they tend to be strongest when fear runs highest,” he detailed. “This month, bitcoin has been dragged around by the AI trade for reasons that have little to do with bitcoin itself. But the leash pulls in both directions.”

Green concluded:

“As confidence in AI rebuilds, bitcoin is likely to be among the first assets to feel the lift, and quite possibly the one that feels it most.”

title: The 72-Hour Clock: A Realistic GDPR Breach Emergency Plan for the Agentic AI Era
summary: GDPR gives you 72 hours to report a data breach. Here's what crypto firms must do: who to notify, where to file, and how to protect users.
content:
This is the guide I wish I had when I dealt with a large GDPR incident not too long ago. I went looking for a clear, practical playbook and found almost nothing online: legal texts, regulator forms, and a lot of guesswork. I learned most of what follows the hard way. I hope it helps you find your way faster.

General information only, not legal advice. See the important notice at the end of this guide. Need help with a GDPR breach response plan? Get in touch at Advoqua.

Key Takeaways

  • You have 72 hours from becoming aware of a breach to notify your data protection authority, and weekends count. If you’re late, file anyway and explain why.
  • Where you file depends on whether you have an EU establishment. If you do, you file once, with your lead authority. If like most crypto companies, you don’t, you’re supposed to file in every country where affected users live. The UK and Switzerland need separate filings.
  • If you cannot submit filings within 72 hours in every country where users are affected, prioritize the countries with the highest number of affected users, then work through the remaining countries. Submit brief initial filings and supplement them later.
  • Shopping for a lenient regulator mostly doesn’t work.
  • In crypto, leaked data turns into phishing and physical threats. Tell users fast, and tell them exactly what to do. This will save you major headaches in the future.
  • If you’re MiCA regulated and/or based in the EU, check whether DORA or NIS2 also apply. They run on their own clocks.

Every leader I talk to has a security plan. Very few have a breach plan. Those are not the same thing.

A security plan keeps attackers out. A breach plan is what you do in the 72 hours after they got in anyway. Your engineers are still arguing about scope. Your lawyers are asking whether it is “really” a breach. And a regulator somewhere in Europe is already owed a phone call, whether you know it or not.

That gap matters more now than ever. Attackers increasingly run campaigns with AI agents that scan, exploit and exfiltrate at machine speed. The European paperwork window has not moved: 72 hours. And if you run a platform with real users, some of them are in the EU, and the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) almost certainly follows them to your servers.

What follows is the plan I would want on my desk. It does not try to follow GDPR to the letter. It covers the basics, in order, so you stay on the right side of your regulator and, more importantly, so your users do not pay for your bad week.

Why this matters now (skip if you don’t want context)

DLA Piper’s January 2026 survey recorded 443 breach notifications a day to European regulators, and that counts only the companies that chose to report.

The survey found daily notifications rose 22% in a year, from 363 to 443, the first time above 400 since GDPR took effect in 2018. It also put fines at about €1.2 billion in 2025 and €7.1 billion since 2018.

The headlines match the numbers. TechCrunch’s running list of 2026’s worst hacks includes data on more than 30 million students and staff stolen from Instructure’s Canvas platform, and 15 million people’s health data taken from insurer DentaQuest. One vendor, Klue, was breached through a credential it had issued in 2022 for a limited pilot. The stolen data, including keys to customers’ cloud services, touched close to 200 companies.

Now add AI agents to the picture. In November 2025, Anthropic reported a state-sponsored group that used its Claude Code tool to attack about 30 organizations. By Anthropic’s estimate, the AI did 80 to 90% of the work, at peak firing off multiple requests per second. Humans stepped in at only a handful of decision points.

The agents inside your own company, and the systems around them, are attack surface too. In spring 2026, attackers exploited an account-verification flaw in Instagram’s AI-assisted recovery process, potentially affecting more than 20,000 accounts. In August 2025, attackers used stolen OAuth tokens from the Salesloft Drift chat integration to export data from numerous Salesforce instances. Every agent, bot and integration holding a key to your data is a potential insider, and so is every check built around it.

And yes, this is your problem even if you have no office in Europe. Under Article 3(2), GDPR applies to any company that offers goods or services to people in the EU, or monitors their behaviour there. A crypto exchange, a wallet app or a news site running analytics on EU readers is very likely in scope.

Step 1: The first hours. Contain, preserve, start the clock

The 72-hour clock under Article 33 starts when you become aware of a personal data breach, not when your investigation is finished.

I don’t suggest trying to get smart with what “aware” means. European regulators treat you as “aware” once you are reasonably certain that a security incident has compromised personal data. You get a short window to investigate. You do not get to ignore an alert, wait for Monday or hold out for a forensic report. Weekends and holidays count. Unfortunately I’ve seen awareness of data breaches happening on a Friday afternoon. Guess what, if you’re a stakeholder you’re working non-stop on this for the next 72 hours.

Here is what has to happen before anyone debates whether it is “really” a breach:

  1. Contain. Revoke the compromised passwords, API keys and OAuth tokens. Disable or sandbox every AI agent, bot and integration that touched the affected systems. Isolate infected machines, but do not wipe them.
  2. Preserve evidence. Snapshot access logs, cloud audit logs and your agents’ prompt and tool-call histories. You cannot tell a regulator what was taken if you erased the trail.
  3. Assemble the team. You need an incident lead with real authority (I suggest your Head of Engineering), your compliance officer (or data protection officer if you have one), outside privacy counsel ASAP (will be absolutely a game changer in helping with filings), marketing or communications lead, and one executive who can sign a regulator filing at 2 a.m. Name backups for each.
  4. Open the breach log. Write down the moment you became aware, and every decision after it with the reason. Article 33(5) requires this record for every breach, even ones you never report.
  5. Call your vendors and your insurer. A processor that becomes aware of a breach affecting personal data it processes for you must notify you without undue delay under Article 33(2), whether or not it caused the incident. Most cyber insurance policies also require prompt notice and use pre-approved responders.
  6. Lock down communications. One spokesperson, no speculation. And nobody touches a ransom demand without counsel and law enforcement in the room.

The agentic-era addition is simple: know what your agents can reach before the bad day comes. Keep a live inventory of every AI agent and integration, the data it can read and the keys it holds, and a tested way to switch each one off in minutes.

Step 2: Decide what you owe, and to whom

GDPR sets two different bars: tell the regulator unless the breach is unlikely to put anyone at risk, and tell the people themselves when the risk is high.

First, confirm it is a personal data breach. Article 4(12) covers any security failure that leads to personal data being destroyed, lost, altered, disclosed or accessed without authorization. That includes ransomware that locks data without stealing it. Losing access is a breach too.

Who you tellWhen you mustDeadlineArticle
Your lead or local data protection authorityUnless the breach is “unlikely to result in a risk” to peopleWithin 72 hours of awareness. If later, explain why. Details can follow in phases33(1), 33(4)
The affected usersWhen the breach is “likely to result in a high risk” to themWithout undue delay34(1)
Your internal breach registerEvery breach, reportable or notAs it happens33(5)

To judge the risk, look at what leaked and whose it was. Sensitive data, large volumes, data that easily identifies people and vulnerable users all push the risk up. For a crypto platform, identity documents plus home addresses plus account balances is a target list. Treat that as high risk by default.

You can skip telling users in three cases under Article 34(3). The data was strongly encrypted and the key is safe. You have already acted so the high risk is no longer likely. Or individual notice would take disproportionate effort, in which case a public notice replaces it.

When the reporting threshold is genuinely uncertain, assess promptly and document the decision either way. Failing to notify when you should have can cost a fine of up to €10 million or 2% of global annual turnover under Article 83(4). If the underlying security failure breaks GDPR’s core principles, the ceiling rises to €20 million or 4%.

Regulators do fine for the paperwork alone. Ireland’s Data Protection Commission fined Twitter €450,000 in 2020 for notifying late and documenting poorly. The Dutch authority fined Booking.com €475,000 in 2021 for reporting a breach weeks after it learned of it. And in Meta’s €251 million breach decision in December 2024, €11 million was for an incomplete notification and a thin breach record.

At 72 hours, file what you know: what happened, roughly how many people and records, the likely consequences, what you are doing about it, and a contact. Say clearly that more information will follow. A partial filing on time beats a perfect one late.

Step 3: Work out where to file

Where you file depends on where you are established in Europe, not on where your headquarters sits or where most of your users live.

If you have a “main establishment” in the EU, the one-stop-shop rule in Article 56 gives you a single lead supervisory authority. That is the regulator in the country where your EU decisions about personal data are actually made. A letterbox office does not count.

If you have no EU establishment, which describes many offshore crypto platforms, there is no one-stop shop. Since the European Data Protection Board updated its breach notification guidelines in March 2023, a non-EU company must notify the authority in every member state where affected users live. Appointing an EU representative under Article 27 does not change that.

In practice, a breach that touches users in 12 EU countries means 12 filings, plus one in the UK. Here is how to keep that from eating your 72 hours:

  • Build a residency map now. Count your users by country from KYC, billing and IP data, and refresh it monthly. During a breach you need affected-user counts per country in hours, not days.
  • Know your German authority. Germany has a federal commissioner plus 17 state authorities across its 16 states (Bavaria has two), and for most private companies the state authority is the one that counts. The federal office keeps a list of the state authorities.
  • Pre-translate your filing. Most authorities take notifications through an online form, often in the national language. Draft a template once, translate it, and keep it with your runbook.
  • Bookmark the portals. The appendix at the end of this piece lists every EU, EEA, UK and Swiss authority with its website.

The UK: same rules, separate filing

If the breach touches UK users, you owe a second, separate notification under UK GDPR, on the same 72-hour clock.

After Brexit, the UK kept a copy of GDPR, now called UK GDPR, alongside its Data Protection Act 2018. The rules mirror the EU’s, but enforcement is entirely separate. An EU filing does not cover the UK, and a UK filing does not cover the EU. A company outside the UK that serves UK users is in scope, and usually needs a UK representative too.

The regulator has also changed its name. Under the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, the office of the Information Commissioner was abolished on 30 September 2026 and replaced by a body called the Information Commission. The Act did not change the 72-hour rule for UK GDPR breaches. Telecoms and internet providers have their own breach rules under the separate PECR regime.

UK fines reach £17.5 million or 4% of global turnover at the top tier. Notification failures sit in the lower tier: £8.7 million or 2%.

Don’t mistake the UK for a soft touch. DLA Piper describes UK enforcement as limited compared with the EU, and in November 2025 more than 70 groups signed an open letter calling for an inquiry into a “collapse in enforcement activity”. But security breaches are the exception. In October 2025 the regulator fined Capita £14 million over a 2023 attack that exposed data on about 6.6 million people. A high-priority alert fired within 10 minutes. The infected device was not quarantined for 58 hours, against Capita’s own one-hour target.

Two other neighbours are worth a line in your runbook. Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein apply EU GDPR in full through the European Economic Area, so treat them as EU countries. Switzerland has its own revised Federal Act on Data Protection. Under its Article 24, you must report a breach to the Swiss regulator, the FDPIC, when it is likely to cause a high risk, and do so as soon as possible.

From experience: when 72 hours is not enough

For a small team, filing with every affected authority within 72 hours is close to impossible, and in my experience the regulators know it.

Remember, this guide is not legal advice, especially this part. It is what I have learned from doing it. Each filing takes real time. Every authority has its own portal, its own form and often its own language. Even with documents prepared in advance, you end up copying and pasting the same facts, field by field, into a dozen clunky web forms, while your engineers are still containing the incident. And yes, some reporting sites don’t even work at times.

So prioritize. Here is the approach I would take:

  1. File first where most of your affected users live. Rank countries by affected users using your residency map, and work down the list. If you have a lead authority, it comes first. Prioritize by users, never by which regulator seems friendliest.
  2. Keep going after hour 72. The deadline passing is not a reason to stop. Finish every remaining country as fast as you reasonably can.
  3. Explain the delay in every late filing. Article 33(1) expects reasons when you are late. Say plainly that the 72 hours have passed, that you were filing in several countries at once and started where most users were affected, and that you are completing the rest in good faith.
  4. Use phased notification. Article 33(4) lets you file what you know now and add details later. A short first filing in each remaining country beats a complete one a week late.
  5. Prepare the copy-paste kit now. Write one master incident summary that maps to the fields most forms ask for: what happened, data categories, approximate numbers, likely consequences, measures taken and a contact. Translate it into your users’ main languages before you ever need it.

Perfection is not what regulators expect. What they expect is that you report, honestly and in good faith. The companies that land in real trouble are the ones that never file at all.

Regulatory arbitrage: what is real and what is a myth

Although it may be tempting (and quite frankly logical), you cannot pick a friendlier regulator after a breach, and the regulator with the gentlest reputation (Ireland) turns out to account for most of the value of Europe’s GDPR fines.

Arbitrage is real in exactly one place: where you set up your EU main establishment. Big Tech chose Ireland, and for years critics called Dublin a soft touch. Then other EU regulators started overruling it through the European Data Protection Board, which pushed decisions like the record €1.2 billion fine on Meta in 2023.

DLA Piper GDPR Fines and Data Breach Survey, January 2026 · 31 EU, EEA and UK authorities; top 12 by fines shown

The chart shows two ways regulators differ. On fines, Ireland stands alone because it supervises most of Big Tech. Large totals alone do not prove a regulator is strict across its whole caseload, but they do end the idea of a safe haven. On breach reporting, the gap is enormous: the Netherlands logs 224 notices per 100,000 people a year, Italy 4. Nobody believes Dutch companies get hacked 55 times more often than Italian ones. The more likely story is that reporting culture, thresholds and enforcement pressure vary by country, and that a great many breaches never get reported at all.

Styles differ too. Spain’s regulator issues the most fines by count, 1,048 by CMS’s tally, but most are small, so smaller companies feel it. Italy’s Garante is Europe’s most aggressive on AI: it briefly blocked ChatGPT in 2023 and fined the maker of the Replika chatbot €5 million in 2025. The UK fines rarely, but hard, when security fails.

So where does that leave a leader?

  • The legitimate play is structural. If you have real EU operations, and a MiCA crypto licence already requires them, put your main establishment where your decisions are really made. Choose for predictability and competence, not leniency.
  • There is no arbitrage in notification. If you have no EU establishment, you file everywhere affected users live. Filing with the friendliest authority and skipping the rest is simply non-compliance.
  • The window is closing anyway. The EU’s new GDPR procedural regulation harmonizes how cross-border cases are run from 2 April 2027, which leaves even less room between regulators.

Step 4: Tell your users, and protect them

Your users pay for a breach long after the regulator closes the file, so the notice to them matters more than the one to the authority.

In crypto, leaked customer data does not stay on a forum. It turns into phishing calls, fake support agents and, increasingly, physical threats. In May 2025, criminals bribed overseas support agents at Coinbase to copy customer records: names, addresses, phone numbers, government ID images and balance snapshots. They then demanded $20 million. Coinbase refused, offered a $20 million bounty instead and committed to reimburse eligible customers who were tricked into sending funds to the scammers.

The physical side is worse. France’s interior minister reported 77 crypto-linked kidnapping and extortion incidents in the first half of 2026, up from 45 in all of 2025. In January 2025, Ledger co-founder David Balland was abducted from his home and held for ransom. Ledger’s own 2020 leak of more than 270,000 customer records still fuels scams today. A home address sitting next to an account balance is a safety issue, and that is “high risk” under Article 34 by any reading.

A good user notice is plain, specific and fast. It should cover:

  1. What happened and when, in plain language, not legal prose.
  2. Exactly what was exposed, and what was not. If passwords, private keys and funds were untouched, say so clearly.
  3. The likely consequences. Explain what the exposure could mean for them in practice.
  4. What you have done, and will do. Describe the steps you have taken or plan to take to deal with the breach and reduce the harm.
  5. What scammers will try next. State that you will never call to ask them to move funds, share a seed phrase or install software.
  6. What to do now. Change passwords, switch to app-based or hardware two-factor authentication, and ask their mobile carrier to lock their number against SIM swaps.
  7. Protective steps tailored to what was exposed. Where identity, home addresses or holdings are involved, give specific account-security and personal-safety guidance. Any instruction about moving assets should be verified independently through trusted channels.
  8. Where to get help. A dedicated page, a support line staffed by humans and a contact for your data protection officer.

Do not write “no evidence of misuse” unless you have actually looked. Do not bury the notice in a Friday-night blog post. Publish one dated page and keep updating it, but treat it as support for your direct notices: where individual notice is required, a webpage alone ordinarily does not satisfy it. Attackers now use AI to write convincing phishing from leaked data at scale, so your users need to hear from you before they hear from them.

Other clocks to check

GDPR may not be your only reporting duty. Financial firms, including MiCA-licensed crypto firms, should check DORA, and operators of essential or important digital services should check NIS2. Both run on their own deadlines, some shorter than 72 hours, so have counsel map them before an incident.

Reform is on the way too. The EU’s proposed Digital Omnibus would give companies 96 hours and require notice only for high-risk breaches, but it is not law yet. Plan for 72 hours until the Official Journal says otherwise.

Step 5: After the fire

The regulator’s file stays open long after the incident is contained, and it will judge you on what you wrote down in the first hours.

  • Finish the breach register. Article 33(5) requires the facts, the effects and what you did about them. Meta paid €3 million for a thin record alone.
  • Send follow-ups as you learn more. Article 33(4) allows information in phases. Correct your early estimates openly, and tell every authority the same story. Twelve slightly different versions of one incident is its own problem.
  • Run a post-incident review within 30 days. Find the root cause, and measure the gap between first alert and containment. Capita’s 58-hour gap was one of the failings the regulator cited.
  • Fix the agent layer. Give AI agents the least access they need, short-lived credentials and logged tool calls. Require a human to approve bulk exports. Test them against prompt injection the way you test web apps.
  • Review your vendors. Processors are directly liable for security under GDPR. Require notification without undue delay, with a clear contractual maximum measured in hours.
  • Rehearse. Run a tabletop exercise at least twice a year. Make one of them start at 2 a.m. on a Saturday, with users in 12 countries and a ransom note in the inbox.

The bottom line

A breach can expose weaknesses in both your security and your response. Prompt reporting, clear records and effective remediation matter, but they do not erase failures in how the system was designed or protected.

In the agentic era, a breach is a question of when, not if. Attackers run at machine speed, and your own agents widen the door. What you control is the first 72 hours. Here is the plan to pin to the wall:

  1. Before anything happens: map your users by country, bookmark every regulator’s portal, pre-translate your filing template, inventory every AI agent with a kill switch, and keep one notification matrix covering every regime that applies to you.
  2. Hour 0: log the moment you became aware. Contain, preserve evidence and assemble the team.
  3. Hours 0 to 24: assess the risk, and check whether DORA or NIS2 also apply.
  4. By hour 72: file with your lead authority. With no EU establishment, start where most affected users live, and keep filing past hour 72 with reasons for the delay. File separately in the UK.
  5. As soon as possible, for Switzerland: if the breach is likely to cause Swiss users a high risk, report it to the FDPIC. Swiss law sets no fixed 72-hour window.
  6. Without undue delay: tell affected users in plain language, with concrete steps to protect themselves.
  7. After: send follow-ups, complete the breach register, fix the root cause and rehearse again.

Your users trusted you with their data. In crypto, they may have trusted you with their safety too. Being ready is how you honor that.

Important notice

Breach obligations turn on the facts and on the laws of each country involved, so get advice from qualified counsel in every relevant jurisdiction before you act.

title: Privacy coins face diverging fortunes as KuCoin moves to drop Monero
summary: As KuCoin joins exchanges dropping Monero ahead of new EU restrictions, Grayscale argues that Zcash’s privacy design sets it apart.
content:
Crypto exchange KuCoin said Thursday it will delist Monero (XMR) on Nov. 30, making it the second major platform this month to drop the privacy coin. Exchange MEXC suspended XMR spot trading and delisted its perpetual futures contracts earlier in November.

KuCoin has already suspended XMR deposits and plans to close withdrawals on Dec. 31. XMR fell 10.5% to $449.98 as of 7:00 p.m. UTC on Thursday. The drop extends a decline from about $625 on Nov. 3.

The delisting comes as the European Union prepares to restrict privacy coins on regulated platforms. Starting July 10, 2027, the bloc’s Anti-Money Laundering Regulation will prohibit financial firms, including crypto asset service providers, from maintaining anonymous accounts or accounts that obscure transactions through “anonymity-enhancing coins,” regardless of whether the privacy features are enabled by default or optional. The regulation does not prohibit individuals from holding privacy coins in self-custody wallets.

Launched in 2014, Monero conceals transaction amounts and the wallet addresses of senders and recipients by default. Unlike Monero, Zcash (ZEC), launched in 2016, allows users to choose between transparent and shielded transactions. Both cryptocurrencies have faced regulatory scrutiny over the past few years, with Binance delisting Monero in 2024 and Kraken ending support for it in the European Economic Area later that year.

Zach Pandl, head of research at Grayscale, which launched the first US spot ZEC exchange-traded fund (ETF) in August, said Zcash is positioned differently from Monero. He told Cointelegraph that the firm’s commitment to Zcash will continue for “many years to come.”

Delistings mount ahead of EU privacy coin restrictions

KuCoin’s delisting of Monero follows a series of similar moves by crypto exchanges amid growing regulatory pressure on privacy coins. Since 2018, when Japan’s Financial Services Agency pressed exchanges to drop anonymity coins, regulators in other jurisdictions, including South Korea and Dubai, have also taken steps to restrict their use or availability.

In Europe, plans to restrict privacy coins emerged as early as 2022, when a leaked draft of an Anti-Money Laundering bill came to light. The EU’s regulation defines “anonymity-enhancing coins” as cryptocurrencies with built-in features that anonymize transaction data “either systematically or optionally,” which could bring cryptocurrencies with opt-in privacy features, such as Zcash, within the scope of the restrictions.

Related: Bitwise seeks Texas Stock Exchange listing for Zcash ETF

Pandl said that viewing keys allow Zcash holders to disclose transactions “to an auditor or regulator, law enforcement if they need.” He said the feature gives users greater control over who can access their financial information. “That is exactly how the financial system works today. It’s just that it gives the authority to individuals rather than institutions,” he said.

However, whether viewing keys alone can satisfy regulatory requirements remains a point of debate.

Other approaches to privacy are gaining traction among traditional financial institutions looking to use public blockchains. In April, Paris-based digital asset infrastructure provider Dfns partnered with cryptography firm Zama to bring confidential transactions to its more than 400 enterprise clients, including banks, fintechs and custodians. The collaboration uses encryption to conceal transaction amounts and balances on public blockchains while allowing authorized parties to access the information for compliance purposes.

Grayscale says shielding beats obfuscation

Grayscale has offered exposure to ZEC since the launch of its Zcash Trust in 2017, based on the view that transaction privacy would be essential for financial institutions to adopt public blockchains.

Pandl said that as AI has advanced, it has become “much easier to link pseudonymous addresses with offchain information.” Monero, he explained, uses ring signatures that obscure the source of transactions among multiple possible signers, a method Pandl said “may be vulnerable” as AI-powered blockchain analytics improve.

“We believe strongly that Zcash is the stronger tech,” he said, because “it takes a shielding approach rather than an obfuscation approach.” Zcash uses zero-knowledge proofs to verify shielded transactions without publicly revealing sensitive transaction data onchain.

Monero developers, however, are working on an upgrade that would replace ring signatures with a zero-knowledge proof system in a bid to enhance transaction privacy.

“For public blockchain technology to become a mainstream part of the financial system, it absolutely needs a privacy layer,” Pandl said.

ETF conviction despite outflows

Grayscale’s Zcash ETF began trading on NYSE Arca on Aug. 25, following the conversion of its Zcash Trust. While investors seeking to use Zcash’s privacy features would need to hold the cryptocurrency directly, “the ETF can provide the store of value use case of these [privacy] technologies,” Pandl said.

Grayscale’s ETF reached $1 billion in assets under management on Sept. 24, but that figure had fallen to $406 million on Wednesday. Zcash more than tripled in value this year, rising to $1,653 on Sept. 26 from $524 on Jan. 1, according to Token Terminal data. Its price more than doubled in the month following the ETF’s launch but has since fallen back to $770. The cryptocurrency remains up about 50% year to date.

Pandl described Zcash’s price appreciation over the past year as “Bitcoin’s Solana moment,” referring to Solana’s growing market cap and its challenge to Ethereum’s dominance as the “leading smart contract platform.”

“At 1.2% of Bitcoin’s market cap, I would still consider Zcash at a relatively low value,” he said, adding that Grayscale has no price targets for ZEC.
